frontExample: There was an awkward silence after his comment.
meaning: Uncomfortable, embarrassing, or difficult in a social situation.
nativePronunciation: /ˈɔkwɚd/ — the stress is on the first syllable. The second syllable is weak and reduced.
spanishPronunciation: Keep the second syllable weak. Use an American r without tapping or trilling it as in Spanish. Do not add a vowel after the final d.
examples: I always feel awkward when I don’t know anyone at a party.
The conversation got awkward when they started arguing.
That was an awkward moment, but everyone eventually laughed about it.
She’s gotten less awkward in meetings as she’s become more confident.
usageNote:
Awkward describes a situation or person that feels uncomfortable or socially difficult.
✅ “I felt awkward.”
✅ “It was an awkward conversation.”
Do not confuse awkward with embarrassed.
Awkward describes the uncomfortable situation or feeling.
Embarrassed specifically means feeling ashamed or self-conscious.
spanishTranslation: incómodo / vergonzoso / torpe socialmente, depending on context

frontExample: Long meetings can be mentally draining.
meaning: Making you feel very tired, emotionally exhausted, or low on energy.
category: Adjective — present participle form of drain used as an adjective
nativePronunciation: /ˈdreɪnɪŋ/ — the stress is on the first syllable. The ending -ing is /ɪŋ/, not /in/.
spanishPronunciation: The vowel /ɪ/ in -ing differs in quality from Spanish /i/, not just in length. End with the nasal /ŋ/ at the back of the mouth, without a separate hard g sound.
examples: Dealing with constant complaints is emotionally draining.
Yesterday’s meeting was really draining.
This project has been draining lately, but we’re almost finished.
Working long hours without breaks can become physically and mentally draining.
usageNote:
Draining describes the thing that causes tiredness.
✅ “The meeting was draining.”
Drained describes how a person feels afterward.
✅ “I felt drained after the meeting.”
❌ “I felt draining after the meeting.”
spanishTranslation: agotador / desgastante / que te deja sin energía

frontExample: I went straight home after work.
meaning: Went is the past simple form of go. It means that someone moved, traveled, or proceeded somewhere in the past.
category: Verb — past simple form of go
nativePronunciation:
/wɛnt/ — one syllable. The vowel is /ɛ/, like the vowel in bed.
The irregular forms sound very different:
- go /ɡoʊ/
- went /wɛnt/
- gone /ɡɔn/
spanishPronunciation: Start with /w/ without adding a g before it. The vowel /ɛ/ is more open than Spanish /e/. Keep the final /nt/ cluster and do not add a vowel after t.
examples: I usually go to the gym after work.
We went out for dinner last night.
She’s already gone home.
He goes to that coffee shop almost every morning.
usageNote: Use went for the past simple: “I went there yesterday.” After have/has/had, use a past participle: “She has gone home.” Do not say “She has went home.” For completed visits, been is often clearer: “I’ve been there several times.” Went, gone, and been are not interchangeable.
spanishTranslation: fui / fue / fueron / iba, depending on context

frontExample: I keep putting off going to the dentist.
meaning: To delay doing something until a later time, often because you don’t want to do it yet.
nativePronunciation: /pʊt ɔf/ — the base, past, and past participle forms of put are pronounced the same. In connected speech, link put and off without inserting an extra vowel.
spanishPronunciation: Keep /ʊ/ relaxed; it differs in quality from Spanish /u/. Link put and off without inserting an extra vowel, and finish off with /f/.
examples: I usually put off difficult tasks until the last minute.
I put off calling him because I didn’t know what to say.
We’ve put off the meeting until next week.
Don’t keep putting it off—you’ll have to do it eventually.
usageNote:
When put off is followed by another action, use an -ing form, not an infinitive.
✅ “I put off calling him.”
❌ “I put off to call him.”
Because put is irregular but does not change form:
“I put off the appointment yesterday.”
“We’ve put off the meeting twice.”

meaning: In this context, fuel means to provide energy, motivation, or support that makes something stronger or keeps it growing.
nativePronunciation: /ˈfjuːəl/ — usually pronounced with two quick syllables. The first syllable contains /fjuː/, similar to few.
spanishPronunciation: Move smoothly from /f/ into the /j/ sound, like the y in yes. Keep the weak second vowel /ə/ short and relaxed; do not turn it into a strong open vowel.
examples: Positive feedback often fuels my motivation.
His criticism fueled her determination to prove him wrong.
The recent success has fueled even more interest in the project.
Constant rumors can fuel unnecessary conflict at work.
usageNote:
Fuel can be both a noun and a verb, but on this card it is used as a verb.
As a noun:
“We need more fuel for the car.”
As a verb:
“Competition fuels innovation.”
Regular past form:
“The announcement fueled speculation.”
In American English, fueled is usually spelled with one l.
spanishTranslation: impulsar / alimentar / fomentar / dar energía a
